meta.titre: Liquid Mixtures: Raoult's Law, Fractional Distillation and Azeotropes

sections.contenu_markdown: At the refinery in Limbe crude oil is separated by fractional distillation, and in villages of the Grassfields fermented palm wine is distilled into a much stronger spirit. In both cases a mixture of liquids is boiled and the vapour is richer in the more volatile component, which is why repeated distillation separates them. Yet a bottle of spirit never reaches 100% ethanol however carefully it is distilled, because ethanol and water form an azeotrope. Examiners ask about Raoult's law, the shape of boiling-point diagrams and the limits of fractional distillation, so you must be able to calculate with partial pressures and also to explain the behaviour in terms of intermolecular forces.

items: The vapour pressure of a liquid is the pressure of its vapour in equilibrium with the liquid at a given temperature, and a liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure.
The mole fraction of a component is its amount divided by the total amount of all components in the mixture.
A more volatile liquid has weaker intermolecular forces, a higher vapour pressure and a lower boiling point.
Intermolecular forces are London forces, permanent dipole forces and hydrogen bonds, and mixing liquids breaks and forms these forces.

sections.titre: Raoult's law, fractional distillation and azeotropes
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Ideal mixtures.** In an ideal mixture of liquids A and B, the attractions between A and B molecules are the same as those between A and A and between B and B. Mixing then gives no enthalpy change and no change of volume. Each component obeys **Raoult's law**: its partial vapour pressure equals the mole fraction in the liquid times its vapour pressure when pure at the same temperature:

$$
 p_A = x_A\,p_A^{\circ}
$$

The total vapour pressure is the sum of the partial pressures, $P = p_A + p_B$, and the mole fraction of A in the **vapour** is $y_A = p_A / P$. Since the more volatile component has the larger $p^{\circ}$, the vapour is richer in it than the liquid. Hexane and heptane are a good example of a nearly ideal pair.

**Fractional distillation.** The vapour rising in a column condenses on trays or packing, the condensate is re-vaporised, and every cycle enriches the vapour in the more volatile component. Each cycle is a theoretical plate, so a longer or better column gives a purer distillate. The more volatile liquid collects at the top, and the less volatile one stays in the flask.

**Non-ideal mixtures.** Real mixtures deviate from Raoult's law when A-B forces differ from A-A and B-B forces:

| | Positive deviation | Negative deviation |
|---|---|---|
| A-B forces compared with A-A and B-B | weaker | stronger |
| Vapour pressure compared with Raoult | higher | lower |
| $\Delta H$ of mixing | positive (mixture cools) | negative (mixture warms) |
| Volume on mixing | increases | decreases |
| Boiling point diagram | minimum | maximum |
| Example | ethanol and water | nitric acid and water |

At the extreme the boiling-point curve has a minimum or maximum and the mixture at that point is an **azeotrope**.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked what an azeotrope is, or why a mixture cannot be separated completely by fractional distillation.
variantes.contenu_markdown: An **azeotropic mixture** boils at a constant temperature and gives a vapour with exactly the same composition as the liquid. Because the vapour does not differ from the liquid, further evaporation and condensation produce no enrichment, so fractional distillation cannot separate the azeotrope into its components. Ethanol and water form a minimum-boiling azeotrope of about 96% ethanol by mass, boiling at about 78 degrees Celsius. Nitric acid and water form a maximum-boiling azeotrope of about 68% acid, boiling near 121 degrees Celsius.

variantes.nom: Separating and purifying with an azeotrope
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks what is obtained at the top and in the flask, or how to obtain a pure component.
variantes.contenu_markdown: For a minimum-boiling azeotrope, fractional distillation of a mixture that has less ethanol than the azeotrope gives the **azeotrope as distillate**, and the flask ends as nearly pure water. For a maximum-boiling azeotrope, the azeotrope stays in the **flask** and the component in excess distils off first. To obtain absolute ethanol the water is removed chemically: the spirit is refluxed with quicklime, which reacts with water, $\mathrm{CaO(s)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ca(OH)_{2}(s)}$ and the ethanol is then distilled off. Other methods are an added entrainer or molecular sieves.

variantes.nom: Reading a boiling-point against composition diagram
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a diagram is described and you must say what the curves show.
variantes.contenu_markdown: On a graph of boiling temperature against composition there are two curves. The lower curve gives the composition of the **liquid** that boils at a given temperature; the upper curve gives the composition of the **vapour** at that temperature. A horizontal line at a chosen temperature joins them. The vapour is richer in the component with the lower boiling point. Stepping from the liquid curve across to the vapour curve and back down gives one theoretical plate. For an azeotrope the two curves touch at a minimum or maximum.

sections.enonce_markdown:
Liquids A and B form an ideal mixture. At a certain temperature the vapour pressure of pure A is 50.0 kPa and that of pure B is 20.0 kPa. A mixture is made from 2.00 mol of A and 3.00 mol of B.

(a) Calculate the partial pressure of each component and the total vapour pressure above the mixture.

(b) Calculate the mole fraction of A in the vapour.

(c) This vapour is condensed to a liquid, which is then heated to the same temperature. Calculate the mole fraction of A in the new vapour, and say what the calculation shows about fractional distillation.

etapes.action: Find the mole fractions in the liquid.
etapes.justification: $x_A = n_A / (n_A + n_B)$, because Raoult's law uses mole fractions.

etapes.action: Apply Raoult's law to each component.
etapes.justification: Each partial pressure is the mole fraction multiplied by the pressure of the pure liquid.

etapes.action: Add to get the total pressure.
etapes.justification: Partial pressures of gases in the same space add up.

etapes.action: Find the composition of the vapour.
etapes.justification: The mole fraction in the vapour is the partial pressure divided by the total.

The condensate has the vapour's composition, $x_A = 0.625$ and $x_B = 0.375$. The temperature is kept the same here to make the arithmetic simple; in a real column each plate is slightly cooler but the pattern is the same.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The mole fraction of A rises from 0.400 in the liquid to 0.625 and then to 0.806 in the vapour: each evaporation and condensation cycle enriches the vapour in the more volatile liquid A, which is how a fractionating column works.

items.erreur_markdown: Using the masses of the liquids as if they were mole fractions, or the volumes.
items.pourquoi_faux: Raoult's law is written in mole fractions, which depend on the amount of each molecule and not on its mass.
items.correction_markdown: Convert each mass to moles with $n = m/M$ and then $x_A = n_A / (n_A + n_B)$.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing $p_A = p_A^{\circ}$ for the partial pressure above a mixture.
items.pourquoi_faux: The partial pressure of A is lowered because only a fraction of the surface molecules are A.

items.erreur_markdown: "The vapour above an ideal mixture has the same composition as the liquid."
items.pourquoi_faux: The component with the higher vapour pressure contributes a larger share of the vapour. The vapour is richer in the more volatile component.
items.correction_markdown: $y_A = p_A / P$ is greater than $x_A$ when A is more volatile (in the example 0.625 against 0.400).

items.erreur_markdown: "With a longer column and enough patience, any azeotrope can be split by fractional distillation into the two pure liquids."
items.pourquoi_faux: At the azeotropic composition the vapour and the liquid have the same composition, so there is no enrichment however many plates are used.
items.correction_markdown: Fractional distillation of a mixture on one side of the azeotrope gives the azeotrope and one pure component; the other component must be removed by a chemical or other method.

items.erreur_markdown: "A positive deviation from Raoult's law means that A-B attractions are stronger."
items.pourquoi_faux: A vapour pressure higher than predicted means the molecules escape more easily, so the A-B forces are weaker than A-A and B-B.
items.correction_markdown: Positive deviation: weaker A-B forces, $\Delta H_{mix} > 0$, minimum-boiling azeotrope. Negative deviation: stronger A-B forces, $\Delta H_{mix} < 0$.

items.enonce_markdown:
At 323 K the vapour pressure of pure hexane ($\mathrm{C_6H_{14}}$) is 54 kPa and that of pure heptane ($\mathrm{C_7H_{16}}$) is 19 kPa. A mixture contains 86.0 g of hexane and 150 g of heptane and may be treated as ideal. ($\mathrm{C} = 12.0$, $\mathrm{H} = 1.0$.)

(a) Calculate the mole fraction of hexane in the liquid.

(b) Calculate the total vapour pressure at 323 K.

(c) Calculate the mole fraction of hexane in the vapour.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $M(\mathrm{C_6H_{14}}) = 86.0$ and $M(\mathrm{C_7H_{16}}) = 100.0\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$. $n(\text{hexane}) = 1.00\ \mathrm{mol}$ and $n(\text{heptane}) = 1.50\ \mathrm{mol}$, so $x(\text{hexane}) = \dfrac{1.00}{2.50} = \mathbf{0.400}$.

(b) $p(\text{hexane}) = 0.400\times54 = 21.6\ \mathrm{kPa}$; $p(\text{heptane}) = 0.600\times19 = 11.4\ \mathrm{kPa}$; $P = \mathbf{33.0\ kPa}$.

(c) $y(\text{hexane}) = \dfrac{21.6}{33.0} = \mathbf{0.655}$. The vapour is richer in hexane, the more volatile liquid.

items.enonce_markdown:
Liquids A and B are mixed in equal amounts (mole fraction 0.50 each). The pure liquids have vapour pressures of 40.0 kPa and 20.0 kPa at the temperature used, and the measured total vapour pressure of the mixture is 24.0 kPa.

(a) Calculate the total vapour pressure predicted by Raoult's law.

(b) State the type of deviation shown and explain it in terms of intermolecular forces.

(c) State what happens to the temperature on mixing and what kind of azeotrope this system may form.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $P = 0.50\times40.0 + 0.50\times20.0 = 20.0 + 10.0 = \mathbf{30.0\ kPa}$.

(b) The measured pressure (24.0 kPa) is lower than predicted, so this is a **negative deviation**. The molecules of A and B attract each other more strongly than A attracts A and B attracts B, so fewer molecules escape into the vapour.

(c) Forming the stronger A-B forces releases energy, so $\Delta H_{mix}$ is negative and the temperature **rises** on mixing. The system may form a **maximum-boiling azeotrope**.

items.enonce_markdown:
At a temperature T the pure liquids M and N have vapour pressures of 150 kPa and 60 kPa. They form an ideal mixture that boils at T under a pressure of 100 kPa.

(a) Calculate the mole fraction of M in the boiling liquid.

(b) Calculate the mole fraction of M in the vapour.

(c) Two other liquids, X and Y, form a minimum-boiling azeotrope containing 70% X by amount. State what is collected as distillate, and what remains in the flask, when fractional distillation is carried out on (i) a mixture containing 90% X and (ii) a mixture containing 40% X.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The mixture boils when $P = x_M\,p_M^{\circ} + (1 - x_M)\,p_N^{\circ} = 100$. So $150x + 60(1 - x) = 100$, $90x = 40$ and $x_M = \dfrac{4}{9} = \mathbf{0.444}$.

(b) $p_M = 0.444\times150 = 66.7\ \mathrm{kPa}$ and $y_M = \dfrac{66.7}{100} = \mathbf{0.667}$. The vapour is richer in M, the more volatile liquid.

(c) (i) Distillate: the azeotrope (70% X); flask: pure X, since X is in excess of the azeotropic composition. (ii) Distillate: the azeotrope (70% X); flask: pure Y, since this mixture has less X than the azeotrope. In both cases the azeotrope has the lowest boiling point, so it distils first, and neither pure component can be collected as distillate.

items_markdown: Raoult's law: $p_A = x_A p_A^{\circ}$; the total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures and the vapour mole fraction is $y_A = p_A/P$.
The vapour above an ideal mixture is richer in the more volatile component; fractional distillation repeats this enrichment on each theoretical plate.
An ideal mixture has A-B forces equal to A-A and B-B forces, with no enthalpy or volume change on mixing.
Positive deviation (weaker A-B forces) gives a minimum-boiling azeotrope; negative deviation (stronger A-B forces) gives a maximum-boiling azeotrope.
An azeotrope boils at constant temperature with vapour of the same composition as the liquid, so it cannot be separated by fractional distillation alone.
Always convert masses to moles first, and state the temperature to which the vapour pressures refer.
